content:
The stage play "We Are the Happiest," which was canceled by the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority, was brought to Japan by Mount Seen bookstore. Yesterday (the 16th), at Home/Work Village in Setagaya Ward, Tokyo, Japanese actors performed a reading of the translated script, and a creative symposium was also held. Playwright Candace Chong and actor Anthony Wong attended to share their thoughts, with over a hundred Hong Kong and Japanese audience members participating. At the sharing session, when asked about the impact of the work being unable to be performed in Hong Kong, Chong admitted her emotions had been very up and down, and that she sometimes felt very low, but she pointed out that the experience of being banned had given her "valuable life experience," which Anthony Wong described as "immersive learning." Chong said the description was accurate, and added that "the blows you don't see are even more numerous," to which Wong responded, "I feel the same." Chong said she hoped that one day she could write about "all the various blows that you don't understand today."

Mount Seen bookstore has set up the limited-time bookstore "Summer Vacation in a Foreign Land" at Home/Work Village in Setagaya Ward, with activities including a two-day reading of "We Are the Happiest."

Enthusiastic audience response leads to additional performance sessions

This performance is a key activity of the limited-time bookstore "Summer Vacation in a Foreign Land (異国の夏休み)" set up in Tokyo from July to September by the now-suspended independent bookstore "Mount Seen bookstore." It is also the latest work by Candace Chong to be performed in Japan, following earlier productions such as "Mortuary," and more recent works like "May 35" and "Wild Boar."

Mount Seen bookstore manager Sharon said the catalyst for this performance was a "telepathic connection" with Candace Chong, as both hoped to bring good things to Japan to share, which led to this reading and symposium. Sharon had worried about ticket sales and did not dare to reserve a venue that was too large, but the over one hundred tickets for the first session sold out within two days, so a final decision was made to add an extra session at the gymnasium within Home/Work Village, and those tickets also sold out within a few days.

Mount Seen bookstore manager Sharon said that she and Candace Chong had a "telepathic connection" and hoped to bring good things to Japan to share, which led to this reading and symposium.

Reading by Japanese actors after translation; Anthony Wong: Emotion has nothing to do with language

"We Are the Happiest" tells the story of a young gay male couple — articled barrister Philip and Ah Sang — whose relationship takes a tragic turn after Philip's boss Neil intervenes. The stage play premiered in 2022 and was originally scheduled for a rerun at the end of last year, but the West Kowloon Cultural District management said it had received complaints that the play "promotes confrontation and disparages Hong Kong," and canceled the venue and performance.

For this performance, Hong Kong director Indi Chan, based in Japan, condensed the original two-hour production into a one-hour reading. Three Japanese actors — Egami Shingo (playing Neil), Nakanishi Ryosuke (playing Phillp), and Kikuchi Kanki (playing Ah Sang) — performed the translated Japanese text in reading format. After the reading concluded, playwright Candace Chong and Anthony Wong, who was originally scheduled to play Neil in the play, held a creative sharing session with the director and actors.

Three Japanese actors performed the translated Japanese text in reading format.

Among the ticket-buying audience, approximately one-third were from Hong Kong, with the remainder being Japanese audience members. While watching the performance, many audience members opened Chinese or Japanese script collections to read along with the actors' reading, and Anthony Wong was among them. During the sharing session, he recalled that a teacher during his time at the Academy of Performing Arts had taught him that "emotion has nothing to do with language." He said it was his first time following a performance in a foreign language while reading a Chinese script, and he was surprised that despite not knowing Japanese, he could follow the pace of the performance, giving high praise to the outstanding performances of the three Japanese actors.

During the performance, many audience members, including Anthony Wong, opened Chinese or Japanese script collections to read along with the actors' reading. He was surprised that despite not knowing Japanese, he could still follow the pace of the performance, recalling his teacher's teaching that "emotion has nothing to do with language."

Anthony Wong also expressed his hope that "We Are the Happiest" could have a formal performance in Japan, joking that he would need to learn Japanese in order to play the youthful role in the play. In addition to the symposium, he also welcomed collaboration with Japanese arts sector professionals in areas such as performance. This time he also brought eight paintings to participate in "Summer Vacation in a Foreign Land," hoping to hold a solo painting exhibition in Japan next year.

This time Anthony Wong also brought eight Matisse-inspired paintings to participate in "Summer Vacation in a Foreign Land," hoping to hold a solo painting exhibition in Japan next year.

Candace Chong: Gains life experience from being banned; Anthony Wong: Immersive learning

When asked how the inability to perform the work in Hong Kong affected her creative work, Chong responded that a public performance allows her to review the presentation of the text, which is "the final step in a playwright's creative learning process." The inability to stage a production dealt a major blow to her, who loves the stage: "My emotions have been very up and down; I'm a bit happier now that I'm in Japan, but sometimes I feel very low." As for how she creates under such circumstances, she said she is still "adjusting," but that even without being able to perform, she can continue to write, and she is still working on creative projects.

Chong shared her resonance with the author of "Things in nature merely grow," whose two sons died by suicide, while reading the book, emphasizing that the experience of being banned had given her "a different feeling of understanding other people's experiences," and had given her "valuable life experience." Anthony Wong said this was "immersive learning," which drew laughter from the audience. Chong also laughed and said the description was very accurate, because "the blows you see are only the blows you see; in every aspect of my life, the blows you don't see are even more numerous." Anthony Wong responded, "I deeply empathize with your misfortune." Chong stated directly, "All the various blows that you don't understand today, one day in the future, I hope I can write them down," and said she would write them down together with Anthony Wong's share.

After the reading concluded, playwright Candace Chong and Anthony Wong, who was originally scheduled to play Neil in the play, held a creative sharing session with the director and actors.

Candace Chong points to regression in the situation for homosexuals; Anthony Wong uses the cha-cha as a metaphor

Nakanishi Ryosuke, who played Phillp, said that participating in "We Are the Happiest" reminded him of the Japanese literary masterpiece "The Tale of Genji" from over a thousand years ago, in which characters who cannot attain love either kill others or kill themselves. He had previously had doubts about such depictions, but upon finding that a thousand years later, this script from Hong Kong also contained similar plot elements, he said he "began to somewhat understand this state of mind." Chong explained that although the protagonists are homosexuals, the story's exploration of the obsession with love and desire transcends both sexual orientation and national boundaries.

In response to the different performance location, Indi made changes to the original final act and added legal background related to homosexuals in Hong Kong and Japan. At the sharing session, Indi mentioned that "whether in Hong Kong or Japan, same-sex couples are still not able to marry under the law," and urged the audience to continue paying attention to their rights. Chong felt that in the area of homosexuality, Hong Kong had "regressed in many aspects" compared to other places, and she did not dare to say that the next generation would be more open. Anthony Wong used the cha-cha as a metaphor, saying that "the pattern of social development is not a straight line," and that having advances and setbacks is the norm.

An audience member wearing a commemorative T-shirt for "We Are the Happiest" asked questions to Anthony Wong and Candace Chong.

Audience: As long as it's a good work, there will be people who appreciate it

Japanese audience member Ms. Nakamura Miona, who had previously purchased tickets for the originally scheduled West Kowloon performance, said after participating in the event that "I am very happy to be able to see the Japanese actors' interpretation in Tokyo, but it also brings back the feeling of not being able to see the performance in Hong Kong at that time." She said she was curious how Anthony Wong would interpret the role of Neil, and looked forward to the opportunity to see a complete version of the stage performance in Japan.

Hong Kong audience member Ms. So, who had also previously purchased tickets for "We Are the Happiest," specially extended her stay in Japan to participate in this symposium. Ms. So believes that this performance is an example of how there are still many people finding different spaces to demonstrate their strength: "As long as it's a good work, there will be people who appreciate it. Regardless of where it is or in what form, it can touch other people."
